title: Factory Method pattern
idea: The Factory Method pattern lets a base class run a fixed workflow while subclasses decide which concrete object it creates, through one overridable creation method.

analogy.text: A coffee chain gives every branch the same recipe card, but each branch buys milk from its local dairy. The recipe never names the supplier.
analogy.breaks: A branch can switch dairies daily; a subclass's choice is fixed in code.

points: The creator runs the workflow and calls an abstract method to get its product.
Each subclass overrides that method and decides which concrete product to return.
A new variant is a new subclass; the tested workflow is never edited (OCP).
`Collection.iterator()` is one: each collection returns its own iterator class.

hero.title: Class diagram of the import job

edges.label: calls run()
edges.caption: The caller holds an `ImportJob` and calls `run`. It never names a parser class.

edges.label: extends
edges.caption: `CsvImportJob` inherits the whole workflow and overrides only `createParser`.

edges.label: uses
edges.caption: Inside `run`, the creator calls `createParser()` and talks to the result as a `RowParser`.

edges.label: creates
edges.caption: The override returns a `CsvParser`. This is the one decision the subclass makes.

edges.label: implements
edges.caption: `CsvParser` implements `RowParser`, so the creator's code works with it unchanged.

edges.label: extends
edges.caption: Supporting XML is one new subclass. `ImportJob` and `CsvImportJob` are not touched.

code.title: The problem: one switch
code.caption: Creation and use in one method: each new format edits and retests shared code.

walk.text: Callers pass a format string; the service decides everything inside one method.
The CSV parsing logic is welded into the `switch`, next to every other format.
JSON lives in the same method, so a JSON change risks breaking CSV.
XML needs a new `case`: editing a class that already works, which breaks the OCP.
Nothing warns at compile time. The unsupported format fails only when it runs.

code.title: The fix: factory method
code.caption: `ImportJob` owns the workflow; each subclass picks its parser through `createParser()`.

walk.text: The product interface. The creator depends on this, never on a concrete parser.
`run` is `final` and validates input, so no subclass can skip or reorder the workflow.
The factory method: an abstract hook the workflow calls at exactly one point.
A concrete creator is tiny. Its only decision is which product to return.
XML arrived as a new class. No existing class was opened or retested.
Products can be shared: two creators reuse `RegexParser` with different patterns.
Blank input is rejected by the shared workflow, once, for every format.

pitfalls: Calling the factory method from the creator's constructor runs subclass code before its fields are initialised.
Calling `List.of` an example of this pattern is wrong; it is a static factory method.
Dozens of variants means dozens of subclasses; a map of suppliers may fit better.

quiz.q: Using the demo's `ImportJob`, what does this print?
quiz.why: `run` only calls `createParser()`. Dropping the header lives in `CsvParser`, and `RawJob` returns its own parser, so all three lines become rows.

takeaway: Subclasses choose the product; the base class keeps the workflow.

starters: How is the Factory Method pattern different from a static factory method?
